items.name: 鍾祐霖
items.note:
A Few Useful Things to Know about Machine Learning

This article focus on things to beware of when applying machine learning. Most of the things mentioned in the article are based on some mathematical basis and many terms the article uses are of professional terms in the realm of machine learning. As I’m also learning machine learning, I found some of the technical suggestions really helps in the implementation. 

According to this article, I think aside the technical aspect of the algorithm itself, what the HCI researcher can contribute are feature engineering and further research of causation. The article states that the importance of the feature is the key to success in machine learning, and it is often one of the most interesting parts, where intuition, creativity and “black art” are. As a HCI researcher, we know that there is no “black art” in machine learning, the so call “black art” are mostly some human factors and if we gain more knowledge of human and the nature, it is highly possible that we gain more confident on determining which features to represent the data. Also, by the help of machine learning, HCI researchers can get more correlational relationship that can help us to find causal relationships between human behavior and the technologies or any research question we care about.

items.name: 林奕汝
items.note:
Foundations of Statistics – Frequentist and Bayesian 

As the talk Mary Parker, a professor of Mathematics in Austin Community College, gave in the ACCCCESS meeting at AMATYC conference in 2004, most statistics courses in college are about "frequentist" perspective, but a variety of structures have been developed in fact. Bayesian's conclusions are especially easier to understand. By two simple examples, the basic philosophical differences between frequentist and Bayesian statistics includes: 1) Bayesian requires a “prior distribution” on the parameter of interest.  2) Bayesian gave unstable results upon different prior distributions.

In the current Big Data and Machine Learning era, this is an article introducing conservative perspectives. People now would still agree that different people will have different prior distributions. However, even in the author's point, the conclusion depends on their chosen prior distribution, the Bayesian is NOT subjective, because the error rate for known data is evaluated in the same way. Criticism on prior distributions is as unreasonable as arguing the analysis difference between discrete data and continuous data. The assumptions with much more confident now are that the data is representative enough and the conclusion means the best description from those data. As a better description has shown up, of course the conclusion could be updated.

items.name: 王玉美
items.note:
Foundations of Statistics – Frequentist and Bayesian

This article gives a clear explanation about the differences between frequentist and Bayesian approach in the statistical approach. Bayesian approach appears to be subjective because its conclusion depends on the prior distribution and might be unique among each individual. To deal with this issue, people will use flat priors which will give equal weight to all possible values of the parameters. According to the example, it is not surprising that with the same data, people will have different result because people who are using the Bayesian will refer to the prior distribution that might be different between the individuals. But in other words, Bayesian analysis might not be so subjective. The prior distribution is commonly derived from the average of prior belief and even get the standard deviation. Therefore, in the example provided in the paper both of distribution provided by Jose and Vicky are well fit the distribution because the data presented is binominal distribution.

Hence, from this paper, I learn that Bayesian approach can be objective and subjective at the same time. It is also unarguable that Bayesian approach is harder to compute than the frequentist approach. This paper has helped me to understand more about these two approaches and has highlighted those points that are need to be put attention on.

items.name: 楊馥名
items.note:
Foundations of Statistics - Frequentist and Bayesian

I agree with I-Ju and Rosiana in their remarks discouraging the dismissal of Bayesian statistical practice as overly subjective. I believe that the author brings up several useful points to shape the reader's understanding of exactly how nuanced the Bayesian approach can be, and this flexibility is what we need to (importantly) incorporate as much information as possible into statistical analysis when applicable. The approach of "Empirical Bayes" seems rather important in the research case as it emphasizes using cumulative data from multiple, if existing, similar situations to inform the prior distribution used to compute the actual likelihood. This is not very much a "subjective" selection of a prior distribution as it utilizes existing objective information to produce a richer context for the analysis of the present data - frequentist approach does not do this. The ability of Bayesian analysis to contextualize a result seems to be especially powerful in cases where certain fundamental research results are being replicated for robustness.

This conceptual approach to selecting a prior distribution also holds some similarity to that used to select initial probabilities for Hidden Markov Models (HMMs), which model Markov processes with unobserved states - for example, in models used for speech recognition and synthesis the number of states is chosen based on the variability of phonemes in the language, and the initial state emission probabilities are selected based on properties of the training data such as mean and variance. Even though these initialized parameters have to be hand-selected, I would not say they are subjective because they are informed by objective data and information informed by data.

items.name: 鍾祐霖
items.note:
Foundations of Statistics – Frequentist and Bayesian

In this handout the author want to address two statistical approaches which are Frequentist statistics and Bayesian statistics.

Bayesian statistics is attractive when we have relatively small set of data and some knowledge to agree on some prior distributions. This method is quite useful for practical researchers, especially for us HCI researchers, since we often have to do analysis on a limited data we obtain. For example lab experiments or observation records, the number of data often falls into the range of tens at most a hundred and hard to be more. Even with gathering data by questionnaires we are unlikely to obtain more than thousand records. Furthermore, in HCI researches, we often build assumption or hypothesis on some general human behavioral basis that has been research for a long time and thus we have quite a confident prior distribution. In this situation I believe Bayesian statistics is a appropriate method to chose.

Even though I prefer using Bayesian statistics in HCI researches, I have to bare this in mind that theorem is just a tool to help us determine a choice in this uncertain, chaotic world. To evaluate a theorem, we still need a huge amount of data and perhaps many years of research.

items.name: 李若彤
items.note:
A Few Useful Things to Know about Machine Learning

Due to AlphaGo that is a milestone achievement for artificial intelligence, AI has become one of the hot topic. Machine learning grew out of the quest for artificial intelligence. People have increasingly made a beeline for machine learning in recent years. They also attempted to find correlations so as to solve real life problem by machine learning. Yet, correlation does not imply causation is made so often. 

A story of beers and diapers is widely known. Wal-Mart found beer and diaper sales on Friday afternoons were strongly correlated. So, beer and diapers are often bought together at the supermarket, then perhaps putting beer next to the diaper section will increase sales. However, it never happened like that. It’s a great story even though it should be filed under the category of urban legends.

Therefore, before we predict the effects of our actions, do not just refer correlations between observable variables. For complex hypotheses testing and for avoiding the correlation is not causation trap, we should need folks with a strong statistics foundation.

items.name: 李柏翰
items.note:
A Few Useful Things to Know about Machine Learning

Machine learning is a well-know keyword nowadays, especially in the field of computer science, which I noticed that many laboratories has started adopting machine learning to tackle research problem and facilitate the procedure, or even started doing research of machine learning. 

Machine learning can figure out how to perform important tasks by generalizing from sample, however, the very first problem facing you is the increasingly variety of learning algorithms available. Of course, it is thoughtful to try several algorithms, but never forget the purpose of your research, to "generalize from the sample". A beautiful mistake and trap, is that we intensely train with the training data, and resulting in overfitting result that couldn't be generalized to the real world, and it is sort of like making too many random variables fixed in the lab study, which could be less generalizable and looks fake.

items.name: 姚舜懷
items.note:
A Few Useful Things to Know about Machine Learning

Overfitting is a common knowledge in machine learning field. In the paper, the author clearly demonstrates the many faces of overfitting. As I learned from machine learning class in this semester, when we get 100% accuracy on training data but only 50% accuracy on testing data, it is obvious that our classifier is overfitting with training data. The new knowledge I learned from the paper is the other way to analyze overfitting by decomposing generalization error into bias and variance. Moreover, the author also remind us we can use cross validation to combat overfitting.
